title: The Angry Eye

patient.name: Mr Suresh Kumar s/o Selvam
patient.presenting_complaint: Right eye pain, redness, and sensitivity to light for 4 days

history.hpc: Mr Suresh presents with a 4-day history of right eye pain, redness, and severe photophobia. He describes the pain as a deep ache, worse in bright light. His vision has been blurry but not dramatically reduced. There is no discharge. He has had two similar episodes in the past 18 months, both in the right eye, which resolved with eye drops from a private GP. He did not follow up after those episodes. He has a known diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed 3 years ago, currently not on disease-modifying therapy.
history.pmhx: Ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27 positive, confirmed on blood test 3 years ago), no other conditions
history.social_hx: Non-smoker, social drinker, manual labour environment — dust exposure

iop.right: 8 mmHg (low — due to ciliary body inflammation)

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right: ciliary (perilimbal) injection, corneal oedema with fine stellate keratic precipitates (KPs) on inferior corneal endothelium, 3+ cells and 2+ flare in anterior chamber, small posterior synechiae at 6 o'clock, no hypopyon. Left: quiet.

fundus.right: Hazy view due to anterior segment inflammation — no vitreous cells or posterior involvement visible, disc appears normal
fundus.left: Normal disc and macula, clear vitreous

investigations.sacroiliac_xray: Bilateral sacroiliitis — consistent with known ankylosing spondylitis
investigations.fbc_esr_crp: WBC 8.9, ESR 42 mm/hr, CRP 18 mg/L — mild systemic inflammation

diagnosis: HLA-B27-associated recurrent anterior uveitis, right eye, in the context of ankylosing spondylitis.

immediate: Topical prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops: hourly for 48 hours, then taper over 6–8 weeks based on response
Topical cyclopentolate 1% or atropine 1% BD — mydriatic to prevent posterior synechiae and reduce ciliary spasm (pain relief)
Oral NSAIDs (naproxen) continued for systemic ankylosing spondylitis
Urgent referral to rheumatology — patient not on DMARD therapy despite recurrent uveitis; likely needs anti-TNF agent (adalimumab)
follow_up: Review in 1 week: reassess cells, flare, and IOP — steroid response can paradoxically raise IOP
Gradual steroid taper over 6–8 weeks — do not stop abruptly
Break posterior synechiae with intensive mydriatics if present
Rheumatology referral for adalimumab or other anti-TNF therapy to prevent recurrences
Long-term: monitor for steroid-induced cataract and glaucoma with each recurrence
patient_education: Anterior uveitis in HLA-B27/ankylosing spondylitis is episodic — recurrences are common but manageable
Early treatment prevents complications: synechiae, cataract, raised IOP
Report immediately if vision worsens, pain increases, or a new episode occurs in either eye
Anti-TNF therapy (biologic injections) can significantly reduce recurrence frequency
Do not self-medicate with leftover steroid drops — requires supervised tapering

key_points: Elicits photophobia and deep aching pain — distinguishes anterior uveitis from conjunctivitis
Asks about prior episodes and resolution — recurrent unilateral uveitis pattern
Asks about systemic conditions: arthritis, back pain, IBD, skin changes (psoriasis)
HLA-B27 status and ankylosing spondylitis history
No discharge — differentiates from infective conjunctivitis
Slit lamp examination for cells, flare, KPs, and synechiae
Excludes infective causes: syphilis, TB (chest X-ray, QuantiFERON)
Checks IOP — low in active uveitis, risk of steroid-induced rise
Correctly identifies anterior uveitis (not conjunctivitis or keratitis)
Links to HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis
Topical steroids (prednisolone acetate) with taper plan
Rheumatology referral for systemic disease management and biologic therapy
Safety-netting for recurrences and steroid-related complications
